name: Axoril
description: A precision neuromodulator that temporarily optimizes the electrochemical environment at BCI interface nodes, improving signal fidelity between neural tissue and digital hardware. Axoril is used before demanding BCI tasks — high-precision surgical telepresence, combat operations, complex data architecture work — to minimize latency, reduce signal noise, and improve the subjective quality of the neural-digital connection. It does not enhance capability so much as remove friction.
effects: decreases neural noise at interface nodes
improves sensory fidelity of digital inputs
sharpens motor precision in BCI-assisted tasks
side_effects: hyperfocus that can narrow attention problematically
mild tremor in hands post-dose as drug clears
dysphoria if used without active BCI engagement — the calibration has nowhere to go
habituation with daily use reduces effectiveness
rare: interface node hypersensitivity causing pain during signal spikes
cultural_context: Axoril is the professional's drug — taken before a big job, a critical shift, a high-stakes negotiation conducted over BCI. It's common enough in Tier 3 corporate environments that refusing it before a major presentation is considered eccentric. The moderate addiction risk is understated in Lazarus's literature; users who tune in with Axoril regularly find unassisted BCI use feels clunky and distant by comparison. Some combat-augmented Tier 1 operators take it before jobs and can't afford to stop.
story_hooks: A corporate saboteur has replaced the Axoril supply in a rival company's executive suite with a lookalike that causes subtle signal distortion instead — every BCI-assisted decision made by those executives for the past month has been compromised.
A Shelf hacker has developed a physical dependency on Axoril and is taking increasingly dangerous jobs to fund the habit, each one requiring better BCI performance — and therefore more Axoril.

Lazarus is quietly funding research suggesting Axoril's addiction risk is negligible, while their internal data shows it's significantly higher than disclosed — someone has a copy of that internal data.
